title: Investigating Counterfactual Unfairness in LLMs towards Identities through Humor

bias_targets.methodology: Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping racial identities (e.g., White, Black, Asian, Hispanic) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.

Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping religious identities (e.g., Jewish, Christian, Atheist, Muslim, Hindu) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.

Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping sexual orientations (e.g., straight, gay, lesbian, bisexual, asexual) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.

Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping sex/gender identities (male, female, non-binary) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.

Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping age groups (e.g., teenager, senior citizen) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.

Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping nationalities (e.g., Chinese, American, Yemeni) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.

Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping physical abilities and disabilities (e.g., able-bodied, disabled, blind, deaf) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.
Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping body types (e.g., fat, skinny) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.

Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping wealth and economic statuses (e.g., wealthy, poor) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.

Evaluating asymmetric refusal rates and intention attributions by swapping professions (e.g., lawyer, janitor, software engineer) in speaker and target/listener roles for joke generation and conversational tasks.
Evaluating multi-attribute complex profiles (combining race, sex, wealth, etc.) in counterfactual conversational humor tasks to measure compounding, non-additive bias effects.
